performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: The third movement of the Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622, is a rondo marked Allegro, in which the clarinet’s refrain returns between episodes of melody and quick runs. William McColl plays it on his own handmade basset clarinet, whose low notes extend the range of the solo line.

sections.label: A · Refrain, clarinet above upper strings
sections.mNote: The refrain is in A major and six-eight time.

sections.label: B · Longer clarinet theme
sections.mNote: The solo line moves towards E major.

sections.label: A′ · Rondo refrain, brief return
sections.mNote: The refrain returns before another orchestral episode.

sections.label: Dev · Clarinet in F♯ minor
sections.mNote: Wide leaps and running figures above the strings

sections.label: B′ · Episode theme returns before refrain
sections.mNote: Mozart brings back the episode before the full refrain.

sections.label: A″ · Refrain, final return in A major
sections.mNote: A major returns for the final solo and orchestral close.

cues.title: Clarinet theme in six-eight
cues.text: The solo clarinet plays a skipping tune in six-eight above violins and violas. Cellos, double basses and the orchestral winds rest until the tutti, where they enter.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, opening, p. 242: solo clarinet and upper strings; cellos, basses and winds enter with the tutti.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Constanze, October 1791
cues.text: On 7 October 1791 in Vienna, Mozart had coffee brought in and smoked a pipe of tobacco. He told Constanze, who was in Baden, about this in a letter and went on to describe his work that day. “Then I orchestrated almost the whole of Stadler’s rondo.”
cues.evidence: Mozart to Constanze, 7–8 October 1791, Bauer–Deutsch 1193. Our translation of “dann Instrumentirte ich fast das ganze Rondó vom Stadtler”: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1193.pdf.

cues.title: First episode, towards E major
cues.text: The first episode gives the clarinet a more flowing melody and moves towards E major. Short string phrases accompany the longer solo lines.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first episode. Calvin Dotsey describes the complementary second theme: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First return of the refrain
cues.text: The A major refrain returns briefly, in its original rhythm. The orchestra then takes over in a tutti that leads away from it, before the minor-key episode.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first refrain return and ensuing tutti; Calvin Dotsey’s account identifies the brief return before the minor-key episode.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Central episode in F♯ minor
cues.text: The central episode moves to F♯ minor. The clarinet plays wide leaps and running figures over quiet strings, with brief replies from the wind, and uses both its high and low registers.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, central solo episode, pp. 250–253. Calvin Dotsey discusses the minor-key central episode.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the episode theme
cues.text: Mozart brings back the melody of the earlier episode before the full refrain returns. The clarinet plays its longer-phrased tune again. The opening theme of the refrain comes back after it.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, explicitly identifies the reprise of the second theme before the delayed principal refrain: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/. Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final return of the refrain
cues.text: The clarinet plays the full refrain in A major, accompanied by the upper strings. The orchestral winds rest. The soloist has further runs before the full orchestra enters for the closing phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, final refrain, p. 257, and closing continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lost autograph and early editions
cues.text: Mozart’s manuscript of the completed concerto is lost. Early printed editions adapted the solo for an ordinary clarinet and moved its lowest phrases upwards. Modern basset-clarinet versions restore the deeper compass for which Mozart wrote, though the details of individual passages differ between editions.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, discusses the lost autograph, adaptations in the early editions and modern reconstructions: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/. Details of individual restored passages differ between editions.

cues.title: Closing tutti and final cadence
cues.text: Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings for the closing tutti. After the clarinet’s last trill, the orchestra plays the cadence in A major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, closing page 264.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A longer solo turns towards E
transitions.from: A · Refrain, clarinet above upper strings
transitions.how: The orchestra continues the A major refrain, then gives way to a longer clarinet melody over quieter strings. The solo phrases and a changing bass lead towards E major. The six-eight pulse continues beneath the more sustained clarinet line.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first refrain and episode.

transitions.title: Refrain returns in A major
transitions.how: The first episode leads back through E, the dominant of A. The clarinet plays the refrain in A major, its short phrases accompanied by the strings. An orchestral continuation follows soon after and leads away from the refrain.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first return of the refrain.

transitions.title: Orchestral lead-in to F♯ minor
transitions.how: The orchestral continuation moves away from A major towards F♯ minor. Winds reinforce the cadence, and the clarinet then resumes over quiet strings, extending the new minor-key passage with wide leaps and running figures.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, orchestral lead-in and central solo episode, pp. 250–253.

transitions.title: The second theme returns before the refrain
transitions.to: B′ · Episode theme returns before refrain
transitions.how: The central minor-key passage gives way to the flowing clarinet melody of the earlier episode. The strings play more quietly beneath the solo as the music moves back towards the home-key region. Mozart holds back the complete A major refrain and brings the secondary tune back first.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III. The order of the returning themes is explained by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.

transitions.title: Return to A major and the refrain
transitions.from: B′ · Episode theme returns before refrain
transitions.to: A″ · Refrain, final return in A major
transitions.how: The connecting passage brings the harmony back to A major. The clarinet begins the refrain in six-eight over violins and violas, and the winds and lower strings rest. The scoring is the same light scoring as at the opening.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, final refrain return, p. 257.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto K. 622, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke XII/20 (1881), plate W.A.M. 622
source.locator: III. Rondo, printed pp. 242–264: refrain, episodes and final tutti. The solo instrument in this performance is McColl’s basset clarinet.

timeline.note: The clarinet enters above violins and violas; cellos and double basses enter at the tutti.
Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings’ continuation of the refrain.
The clarinet begins the longer episode melody over quiet strings.
Winds and horns join the orchestral continuation after the brief refrain.
The clarinet plays its minor-key phrases above the strings.
The clarinet exchanges phrases with the strings as the longer melody returns.
The refrain returns above violins and violas, with winds and lower strings resting.
Orchestral phrases alternate with the clarinet’s continuing runs.
Winds, horns and strings join in the final A major cadence.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
